Benjamin Thompson, nascido na colônia britânica de Massachusetts e feito conde do Sacro Império em 1791, passou anos a serviço da Baviera e notou o calor gerado ao furar canhões no arsenal de Munique. Para testar, mergulhou um cano de canhão na água e o furou com uma broca propositalmente cega. A água ferveu em cerca de duas horas e meia, e o calor parecia inesgotável. Ele ainda comparou o metal raspado com o restante e não achou mudança física. Se o calor fosse uma substância guardada no metal, não deveria brotar sem fim; para Rumford, a única coisa transmitida ao cano era movimento. Na época, o resultado não foi visto como ameaça ao calórico, e as incertezas do experimento foram muito debatidas, mas ele inspirou Joule e outros em meados do século XIX. A vida do conde foi agitada: lutou ao lado dos britânicos na independência americana, criou uma sopa para os pobres e lareiras que não enchiam a sala de fumaça. Em 1804, casou com Marie-Anne Lavoisier, viúva do químico, e os dois se separaram três anos depois.

fontes.trecho: he supported the Loyalist cause during the American War of Independence, commanding the King's American Dragoons during the conflict. [...] He also invented Rumford's Soup, a soup for the poor [...] The Rumford fireplace created a sensation in London [...] so all the smoke would go up into the chimney rather than lingering and entering the room. [...] in 1804, he married Marie-Anne Lavoisier, the widow of the great French chemist Antoine Lavoisier. Thompson separated from his second wife after three years [...] Rumford's most important scientific work took place in Munich, and centred on the nature of heat, which he contended in "An Inquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat Which Is Excited by Friction" (1798) was not the caloric of then-current scientific thinking but a form of motion. Rumford had observed the frictional heat generated by boring cannon at the arsenal in Munich. Rumford immersed a cannon barrel in water and arranged for a specially blunted boring tool. He showed that the water could be boiled within roughly two and a half hours and that the supply of frictional heat was seemingly inexhaustible. Rumford confirmed that no physical change had taken place in the material of the cannon by comparing the specific heats of the material machined away and that remaining. Rumford argued that the seemingly indefinite generation of heat was incompatible with the caloric theory. He contended that the only thing communicated to the barrel was motion. [...] Count of the Holy Roman Empire, 1791. [...] Born in Woburn, Massachusetts

The caloric theory is a superseded scientific theory that heat consists of a self-repellent fluid called "caloric" that flows from hotter bodies to colder bodies. [...] In his influential 1789 textbook Traité Élémentaire de Chimie, Lavoisier clarified the concept of caloric and introduced it to a wider audience. [...] He had found that boring a cannon repeatedly does not result in a loss of its ability to produce heat, and therefore no loss of caloric. This suggested that caloric could not be a conserved "substance", though the experimental uncertainties in his experiment were widely debated. His results were not seen as a "threat" to caloric theory at the time [...] Rumford's experiment inspired the work of James Prescott Joule and others towards the middle of the 19th century.

gancho: O livro que fundou a termodinâmica, de 1824, teve 600 exemplares pagos pelo próprio autor e quase sumiu das livrarias. Sadi Carnot morreu de cólera aos 36 anos, na obscuridade. Só depois virou o "pai da termodinâmica".
explicacao: Sadi Carnot era engenheiro do exército francês e filho de Lazare Carnot, figura importante do período napoleônico. Em 1824, publicou "Reflexões sobre a potência motriz do fogo", a única obra que lançou. Na época, as máquinas a vapor aproveitavam só uns 5 a 7% da energia do combustível, e ele fez uma pergunta de fundo: existe um limite para o trabalho que se tira de uma fonte de calor? A resposta foi a primeira teoria bem-sucedida da eficiência máxima de uma máquina térmica. Carnot raciocinava com a teoria do calórico, o calor como fluido, embora anotações privadas indiquem que, em 1832, já a tinha abandonado. O livro quase não teve leitores. Em 1832, aos 36 anos, ele morreu de cólera. Em 1834, outro engenheiro, Émile Clapeyron, publicou um comentário detalhado da obra, e foi por ele que William Thomson, o futuro Lord Kelvin, conheceu as ideias de Carnot em 1845. O original, Thomson só conseguiu ler no fim de 1848. Com essa base, Kelvin criou uma escala absoluta de temperatura, e Rudolf Clausius definiu a entropia e formulou a segunda lei da termodinâmica.

fontes.trecho: 1 June 1796 – 24 August 1832), known as Sadi Carnot, was a French military engineer and physicist. [...] In that book, which would be his only publication, Carnot developed the first successful theory of the maximum efficiency of heat engines. [...] Thomson used Carnot's analysis to develop an absolute thermodynamic temperature scale, while Clausius used it to define the concept of entropy, thus formalizing the second law of thermodynamics. Carnot was the son of Lazare Carnot, an eminent mathematician, engineer, and commander of the French Revolutionary Army and later of the Napoleonic army. [...] Carnot died in relative obscurity at the age of 36, but today he is often characterized as the "father of thermodynamics". [...] According to the hospital record, he was cured from "mania" but then died of cholera on 24 August. [...] published in Paris in June of 1824 by Bachelier, with Carnot himself paying for the printing of the 600 copies. The work attracted little attention during his lifetime and virtually disappeared from booksellers and libraries. An article published in 1834 (two years after Carnot's death and ten years after the publication of his book) by the engineer and fellow polytechnicien Émile Clapeyron finally succeeded in calling attention to Carnot's work [...] "Is there a limit to the work that can be generated from a given heat source?" [...] the efficiency of a typical engine – the useful work it was able to do when a given quantity of fuel was burned – was only about 5–7%. [...] William Thomson read Clapeyron's paper in 1845, while visiting the Paris laboratory of Henri Regnault, but it was only at the end of 1848 that Thomson was able to read Carnot's original work [...] there is material indicating that Carnot had, by the spring of 1832, rejected the caloric theory and accepted the equivalence of heat and work.

gancho: James Joule, que mostrou que trabalho vira calor e deu nome à unidade de energia, administrava a cervejaria da família. A Royal Society recusou publicar um artigo dele, e na lua de mel ele planejou medir uma cachoeira.
explicacao: Joule nasceu em 1818, filho de um cervejeiro rico, e foi aluno particular de John Dalton. Adulto, cuidava da cervejaria, e a ciência era um passatempo levado a sério. Por volta de 1840, quis saber se os novos motores elétricos poderiam substituir as máquinas a vapor da fábrica, e a pergunta financeira virou outra: quanto trabalho se tira de uma fonte de energia? Em 1843, apresentou seus resultados num encontro científico em Cork e foi recebido com silêncio. No ano seguinte, a Royal Society ouviu um artigo dele, mas recusou publicá-lo, e o texto saiu em 1845 na revista Philosophical Magazine. Seu experimento mais famoso usava um peso em queda para girar pás dentro de um barril isolado cheio de água, que esquentava. Assim ele mediu quanto trabalho mecânico equivale a uma quantidade de calor. Em 1847, casou com Amelia Grimes e, dias depois do casamento, combinou com William Thomson, o futuro Lord Kelvin, de medir a diferença de temperatura entre o alto e o pé da cascata de Sallanches: se trabalho vira calor, a água que despenca deveria chegar um pouco mais quente lá embaixo. Numa carta publicada em 1845, ele já tinha proposto esse teste aos leitores e calculado que o Niágara esquentaria cerca de um quinto de grau Fahrenheit na queda. A tentativa em Sallanches se mostrou impraticável. Hoje a unidade de energia do Sistema Internacional, o joule, leva o seu nome.

fontes.trecho: The SI unit of energy, the joule (J), is named after him. [...] James Joule was born in 1818, the son of Benjamin Joule, a wealthy brewer [...] Joule was tutored as a young man by the famous scientist John Dalton [...] As an adult, Joule managed the brewery. Science was merely a serious hobby. Sometime around 1840, he started to investigate the feasibility of replacing the brewery's steam engines with the newly invented electric motor. [...] However, Joule's interest diverted from the narrow financial question to that of how much work could be extracted from a given source [...] He announced his results at a meeting of the chemical section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in Cork in August 1843 and was met by silence. [...] Joule read his paper to the Royal Society on 20 June 1844, but his paper was rejected for publication by the Royal Society and he had to be content with publishing in the Philosophical Magazine in 1845. [...] involving the use of a falling weight, in which gravity does the mechanical work, to spin a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water which increased the temperature. [...] Joule married Amelia Grimes on 18 August and the couple went on honeymoon. Marital enthusiasm notwithstanding, Joule and Thomson arranged to attempt an experiment a few days later to measure the temperature difference between the top and bottom of the Cascade de Sallanches waterfall, though this subsequently proved impractical. [...] Joule married Amelia Grimes in 1847. [...] He wrote a letter to the Philosophical Magazine, published in September 1845 describing his experiment.

fontes.titulo: On the Existence of an Equivalent Relation between Heat and the ordinary Forms of Mechanical Power, J. P. Joule (Philosophical Magazine, 1845; texto reproduzido no ChemTeam)
fontes.trecho: Any of your readers who are so fortunate as to reside amid the romantic scenery of Wales or Scotland could, I doubt not, confirm my experiments by trying the temperature of the water at the top and at the bottom of a cascade. If my views be correct, a fall of 817 feet will course generate one degree of heat, and the temperature of the river Niagra will be raised about one fifth of a degree by its fall of 160 feet.

gancho: Em 1867, Maxwell imaginou um ser que separaria moléculas rápidas e lentas, esquentando um lado sem gastar trabalho. A saída mais aceita para o enigma: apagar informação produz calor, algo medido em 2012.
explicacao: No experimento mental, um ser minúsculo controla uma portinhola entre duas câmaras de gás e só deixa passar as moléculas rápidas para um lado e as lentas para o outro. Um lado esquenta, o outro esfria, e a entropia total cairia sem gasto de trabalho, contrariando a segunda lei da termodinâmica. Maxwell, que era muito religioso, falava em "ser finito"; quem o chamou de demônio foi Lord Kelvin. Em 1929, Leó Szilárd sugeriu que medir as moléculas custaria energia. Em 1961, Rolf Landauer, da IBM, propôs que o custo inevitável está em outro lugar: apagar um bit de memória libera um mínimo de calor, que cresce com a temperatura. Em 1982, Charles Bennett aplicou isso ao demônio: cedo ou tarde ele enche a memória com o que observou e precisa apagá-la, e esse apagamento paga a conta da entropia. Em 2012, físicos mediram pela primeira vez o calor minúsculo liberado ao apagar um único bit, usando uma partícula num poço duplo. O limite de Landauer é aceito pela maioria, mas pesquisadores como John Earman e John Norton argumentam que a explicação é circular, e o debate continua. À temperatura ambiente, o limite é tão baixo que, em 2012, os computadores gastavam cerca de um bilhão de vezes mais por operação.

fontes.trecho: Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment that appears to disprove the second law of thermodynamics. It was proposed by the physicist James Clerk Maxwell in 1867. [...] Lord Kelvin would later call it a "demon". In the thought experiment, a demon controls a door between two chambers containing gas. As individual gas molecules (or atoms) approach the door, the demon quickly opens and closes the door to allow only fast-moving molecules to pass through in one direction, and only slow-moving molecules to pass through in the other. [...] the demon's actions cause one chamber to warm up and the other to cool down. This would decrease the total entropy of the system, seemingly without applying any work, thereby violating the second law of thermodynamics. [...] The concept of Maxwell's demon has provoked substantial debate in the philosophy of science and theoretical physics, which continues to the present day. [...] In his letters and books, Maxwell described the agent opening the door between the chambers as a "finite being". Being a deeply religious man, he never used the word "demon". [...] One of the most famous responses to this question was suggested in 1929 by Leó Szilárd [...] the act of acquiring information would require an expenditure of energy. [...] In 1982, Charles Bennett showed that, however well prepared, eventually the demon runs out of information storage space and must begin to erase the information it has previously gathered. [...] the minimum heat dissipated by erasing information was experimentally measured by Antoine Bérut et al. in 2012, using a colloidal particle in a double-well potential [...] John Earman and John D. Norton have argued that Szilárd and Landauer's explanations of Maxwell's demon begin by assuming that the second law of thermodynamics cannot be violated by the demon [...] It would therefore be circular to invoke these derived properties to defend the second law from the demonic argument.

Landauer's principle states that the minimum energy needed to erase one bit of information is proportional to the temperature at which the system is operating. [...] As of 2012, modern computers use about a billion times as much energy per operation. [...] Rolf Landauer first proposed the principle in 1961 while working at IBM. [...] In a 2012 article published in Nature, a team of physicists from the École normale supérieure de Lyon, University of Augsburg and the University of Kaiserslautern described that for the first time they have measured the tiny amount of heat released when an individual bit of data is erased. [...] The principle is widely accepted as physical law, but it has been challenged for using circular reasoning and faulty assumptions.

gancho: Há sistemas com temperatura negativa na escala kelvin, e eles não são frios: são mais quentes que qualquer coisa a temperatura positiva. Em contato com um corpo comum, eles cedem calor, nunca recebem.
explicacao: O truque está no que a temperatura mede de fato. Nas temperaturas comuns, as partículas ocupam mais os estados de energia baixa do que os de energia alta. Numa temperatura negativa, essa distribuição se inverte e os estados de energia alta ficam mais cheios. Isso só é possível em sistemas que têm um teto de energia, como spins nucleares num campo magnético. Num gás comum, as partículas podem sempre correr mais, então não há teto e não há temperatura negativa. Perto do teto, colocar mais energia passa a reduzir o número de arranjos possíveis, e a entropia cai: é aí que a temperatura fica negativa. Por isso, ela não está abaixo do zero absoluto, e sim "acima do infinito". Lars Onsager previu a possibilidade em 1949, e os primeiros sinais experimentais vieram em 1951, com Purcell e Pound, nos spins nucleares de um cristal de fluoreto de lítio. O exemplo clássico é a inversão de população dos lasers. Em 2013, uma equipe conseguiu temperatura negativa também no movimento de átomos de potássio-39 presos numa rede de laser.

fontes.trecho: Certain thermodynamic systems can achieve negative thermodynamic temperature; that is, their temperature can be expressed as a negative quantity on the Kelvin or Rankine scales. [...] At ordinary positive temperatures, lower-energy states are more likely to be occupied than higher-energy states. At negative temperatures, this distribution is reversed, so higher-energy states become more populated than lower-energy ones. For this reason, a system with a truly negative temperature on the Kelvin scale is hotter than any system with a positive temperature. If a negative-temperature system and a positive-temperature system come in contact, heat will flow from the negative- to the positive-temperature system. A standard example of such a system is population inversion in laser physics. [...] This is the case for ordinary particles, such as atoms or dust, whose kinetic energy can increase without bound. [...] Negative temperatures are only possible in systems that have a maximum energy they can hold. As such systems approach this maximum energy, the number of accessible states begins to decrease with further increases in energy, causing the entropy to fall and making the temperature negative. Examples of such systems include two-level systems and nuclear spin ensembles in an external magnetic field. [...] The possibility of negative temperatures was first predicted by Lars Onsager in 1949. [...] It seems negative temperatures were first found experimentally in 1951, when Purcell and Pound observed evidence for them in the nuclear spins of a lithium fluoride crystal placed in a magnetic field [...] A substance with a negative temperature is not colder than absolute zero, but rather it is hotter than infinite temperature. [...] Negative temperatures have also been achieved in motional degrees of freedom. Using an optical lattice, upper bounds were placed on the kinetic energy, interaction energy and potential energy of cold potassium-39 atoms. [...] Braun, S.; Ronzheimer, J. P.; Schreiber, M.; Hodgman, S. S.; Rom, T.; Bloch, I.; Schneider, U. (2013). "Negative Absolute Temperature for Motional Degrees of Freedom".

gancho: O lugar natural mais frio que se conhece é uma nebulosa a 5 mil anos-luz. Seu gás se expande tão rápido que esfriou abaixo da temperatura do próprio fundo do espaço, a menos de meio grau do zero absoluto.
explicacao: A Nebulosa do Bumerangue, na constelação do Centauro, é o gás expelido por uma estrela gigante vermelha no fim da vida. O espaço vazio não é totalmente frio: a radiação que sobrou do Big Bang o mantém a cerca de 2,725 graus acima do zero absoluto. Em observações de 1995, astrônomos notaram que a nebulosa absorvia essa radiação, sinal de que estava mais fria que ela. O frio vem da expansão: o gás corre para fora a mais de 150 km por segundo, e um gás que se expande assim, sem receber calor de fora, esfria (é a chamada expansão adiabática). Cálculos de 2017, com o radiotelescópio ALMA, indicam menos de meio kelvin. A estrela sozinha não teria força para lançar tanta matéria tão depressa; a explicação proposta é que uma estrela companheira pequena tenha mergulhado no coração da gigante. O fenômeno é passageiro: a nebulosa já está esquentando aos poucos, e congeladores cósmicos como ele talvez sejam comuns, mas durariam pouco.

fontes.trecho: News Release: June 5, 2017 at 11:00 am EDT [...] An ancient, red giant star in the throes of a frigid death has produced the coldest known object in the cosmos — the Boomerang Nebula. [...] may be that a small companion star has plunged into the heart of the red giant, ejecting most the matter of the larger star as an ultra-cold outflow of gas and dust. This outflow is expanding so rapidly — about 10 times faster than a single star could produce on its own — that its temperature has fallen to less than half a degree Kelvin (minus 458.5 degrees Fahrenheit). [...] The Boomerang Nebula is located about 5,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Centaurus. [...] When the Boomerang Nebula was first observed in 1995, astronomers noted that it was absorbing the light of the Cosmic Microwave Background, which is the leftover radiation from the Big Bang. This radiation provides the natural background temperature of space — only 2.725 degrees above absolute zero. [...] Traveling more than 150 kilometers per second [...] Even now, the Boomerang Nebula is slowly warming. [...] It's possible these super cosmic freezers are quite common in the universe, but they can only maintain such extreme temperatures for a relatively short time.

fontes.titulo: The Coldest Place in the Universe (NRAO Science Highlights)
fontes.trecho: The pre-planetary nebula, the Boomerang Nebula, is the coldest known place in the Universe, refrigerated by an expanding molecular outflow (Joule-Thomson effect), to roughly 1deg K.
making it the coldest natural place currently known. [...] Cooling to sub cmbr temperature is by adiabatic expansion.

gancho: Numa chapa bem quente, uma gota d'água dura mais do que numa menos quente. Em testes do século XIX, uma gota sumiu quase na hora a 168 °C, mas resistiu 152 segundos a 202 °C, flutuando num colchão de vapor.
explicacao: É o efeito Leidenfrost, descrito pelo médico alemão Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost num tratado de 1756. Quando a superfície passa bem do ponto de ebulição, a parte de baixo da gota vira vapor no instante do contato, e esse vapor sustenta o resto da gota logo acima da chapa. Como o vapor conduz calor muito pior que o metal, a gota esquenta devagar e desliza de um lado para o outro. Para a água, o fenômeno começa por volta de 193 °C, mas o ponto exato é difícil de prever e depende da superfície e das impurezas. O efeito preocupava os engenheiros de caldeiras: o engenheiro vitoriano William Fairbairn notou que ele reduzia muito a passagem de calor do ferro quente para a água e citou os testes com aquela gota. O mesmo efeito explica por que gotas de nitrogênio líquido rolam pela pele sem machucar. Em 2009, a equipe do programa MythBusters mostrou que uma pessoa consegue molhar a mão e mergulhá-la rapidamente em chumbo derretido sem se ferir. Não é para tentar em casa.

fontes.trecho: The Leidenfrost effect or film boiling is a physical phenomenon in which a liquid, close to a solid surface of another body that is significantly hotter than the liquid's boiling point, produces an insulating vapor layer that keeps the liquid from boiling rapidly. [...] The effect is named after the German doctor Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in A Tract About Some Qualities of Common Water. [...] If the pan's temperature is at or above the Leidenfrost point, which is approximately 193 °C (379 °F) for water, the water skitters across the pan and takes longer to evaporate than it would take if the water droplets had been sprinkled onto a cooler pan. [...] the bottom part of the water droplet vaporizes immediately on contact with the hot pan. The resulting gas suspends the rest of the water droplet just above it, preventing any further direct contact between the liquid water and the hot pan. As steam has much poorer thermal conductivity than the metal pan, further heat transfer between the pan and the droplet is slowed down dramatically. [...] The temperature at which the Leidenfrost effect appears is difficult to predict. Even if the volume of the drop of liquid stays the same, the Leidenfrost point may be quite different, with a complicated dependence on the properties of the surface, as well as any impurities in the liquid. [...] The effect was also described by the Victorian steam boiler designer, William Fairbairn, in reference to its effect on massively reducing heat transfer from a hot iron surface to water, such as within a boiler. In a pair of lectures on boiler design, he cited the work of Pierre Hippolyte Boutigny (1798–1884) and Professor Bowman of King's College, London, in studying this. A drop of water that was vaporized almost immediately at 168 °C (334 °F) persisted for 152 seconds at 202 °C (396 °F). [...] allowing liquid nitrogen droplets to harmlessly roll off exposed skin. [...] In 1756, Leidenfrost observed that water droplets supported by the vapor film slowly evaporate as they move about on the hot surface. [...] In the 2009 season 7 finale of MythBusters, "Mini Myth Mayhem", the team demonstrated that a person can wet their hand and briefly dip it into molten lead without injury

gancho: Em 1775, o médico britânico Charles Blagden e colegas entraram numa sala a cerca de 127 °C. Ovos assaram até endurecer e um bife ficou quase seco, mas a temperatura do corpo deles mal mudou. O suor era parte do segredo.
explicacao: Os testes começaram em 1774, quando o médico George Fordyce convidou colegas para ver como o corpo resistia a um ar muito mais quente que ele próprio. Já se sabia, por exemplo, que os russos usavam banhos a cerca de 160 graus Fahrenheit. Charles Blagden, que relatou os experimentos à Royal Society, foi aumentando a temperatura. Na sessão mais extrema, um termômetro passou de 260 °F, uns 127 °C, e ele ficou oito minutos lá dentro, de roupa, luvas, meias grossas e um pano diante do rosto para não se queimar com o ferro em brasa que aquecia a sala. Depois de sete minutos, sentiu um aperto no peito e saiu. Para provar que o termômetro não mentia, o grupo deixou ovos e bifes perto dele: em uns vinte minutos, os ovos estavam duros, e em 47 minutos um bife estava cozido e quase seco. Ainda assim, segundo Blagden, a temperatura do corpo deles não mudou de forma sensível. No relato de 1775, ele foi o primeiro cientista ocidental a reconhecer oficialmente o papel do suor no controle da temperatura do corpo. Ele próprio achava, porém, que o suor ajudava muito, mas não explicava todo o resfriamento.

fontes.trecho: Blagden experimented on human ability to withstand high temperatures. In 1775 he showed that human beings could withstand room temperatures as high as 260 degrees Fahrenheit (127 degrees Celsius). In his report to the Royal Society in 1775, he was first Western scientist to officially recognise the role of perspiration in thermoregulation.

fontes.titulo: Further Experiments and Observations in an Heated Room, Charles Blagden (Philosophical Transactions, 1775, texto OCR)
fontes.trecho: without any sensible alteration in the temperature of our bodies. [...] a very large thermometer, placed at a distance from the door of the room, but nearer to the wall than to the cockle, and defended from the immediate action of the cockle by a piece of paper hung before it, rose one or two degrees above $260^\circ$ [...] with the addition, to my common cloaths, of a pair of thick worsted stockings drawn over my shoes, and reaching some way above my knees; I also put on a pair of gloves, and held a cloth constantly between my face and the cockle: all these precautions were necessary to guard against the scorching of the red-hot iron. I remained eight minutes in this situation [...] For seven minutes my breathing continued perfectly good; but after that time I began to feel an oppression in my lungs [...] we put some eggs and a beef-steak upon a tin frame, placed near the standard thermometer [...] In about twenty minutes the eggs were taken out, roasted quite hard; and in forty-seven minutes the steak was not only dressed, but almost dry. [...] probably its effect was very considerable, but by no means sufficient to account for the whole of the cooling

fontes.titulo: Experiments and Observations in an Heated Room, Charles Blagden (Philosophical Transactions, 1775, texto OCR)
fontes.trecho: ABOUT the middle of January, several gentlemen and myself received an invitation from Dr. GEORGE FORDYCE, to observe the effects of air heated to a much higher degree than it was formerly thought any living creature could bear. [...] the Russians use their baths heated to \(60^\circ\) of Reaumur's thermometer, about \(160\) of Fahrenheit's

fontes.titulo: Experiments and Observations in a Heated Room (1774) (The Public Domain Review)
fontes.trecho: In 1774 and 1775 the British physician and scientist Charles Blagden conducted a series of experiments concerned with exploring the effects on the human body of extremely high temperatures [...] Beginning at a modest 100 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius), by the 1775 session they progressed to temperatures upward of a whopping 260 degrees Fahrenheit (127 degrees Celsius).

gancho: O hélio é o único elemento que não congela nem no zero absoluto, se estiver à pressão normal. Para virar sólido, precisa ser espremido a cerca de 25 bar. A culpa é da física quântica.
explicacao: Em 1908, o holandês Heike Kamerlingh Onnes liquefez o hélio pela primeira vez, resfriando o gás abaixo de 5 kelvin. Tentou então solidificá-lo baixando ainda mais a temperatura e fracassou. Não era falta de frio: à pressão atmosférica, o hélio continua líquido até o zero absoluto, algo que nenhum outro elemento faz. O motivo é quântico. Mesmo no frio máximo, os átomos guardam uma energia mínima, a energia de ponto zero, e no hélio ela é alta demais para que se prendam num cristal. A solução veio em 1926, quando Willem Keesom, aluno de Onnes, conseguiu um centímetro cúbico de hélio sólido aplicando pressão. O sólido exige cerca de 1 a 1,5 kelvin e uns 25 bar. Mesmo assim, é difícil distingui-lo do líquido, porque os dois desviam a luz quase do mesmo jeito, e ele é tão compressível que dá para reduzir o seu volume em mais de 30% no laboratório. O hélio líquido mais frio tem outras manias: escapa de recipientes abertos subindo pelas paredes numa película de uns 30 nanômetros.

fontes.trecho: In 1908, helium was first liquefied by Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes by cooling the gas to less than 5 K (−268.15 °C; −450.67 °F). He tried to solidify it by further reducing the temperature but failed, because helium does not solidify at atmospheric pressure. Onnes' student Willem Hendrik Keesom was eventually able to solidify 1 cm3 of helium in 1926 by applying additional external pressure. [...] Unlike any other element, however, helium remains liquid down to a temperature of absolute zero. This is a direct effect of quantum mechanics: specifically, the zero point energy of the system is too high to allow freezing. [...] Helium II will escape from a vessel that is not sealed by creeping along the sides until it reaches a warmer region where it evaporates. It moves in a 30 nm-thick film regardless of surface material. [...] Helium remains liquid down to absolute zero at atmospheric pressure, but it freezes at high pressure. Solid helium requires a temperature of 1–1.5 K (about −272 °C or −457 °F) at about 25 bar (2.5 MPa) of pressure. It is often hard to distinguish solid from liquid helium since the refractive index of the two phases are nearly the same. The solid has a sharp melting point and has a crystalline structure, but it is highly compressible; applying pressure in a laboratory can decrease its volume by more than 30%.

gancho: Existe gelo a milhares de graus. Em 2019, lasers espremeram água a milhões de atmosferas e criaram, por bilionésimos de segundo, um gelo "superiônico", que pode formar uma camada dentro de Urano e Netuno.
explicacao: Gelo é água com as moléculas presas num cristal, e isso não exige frio: basta pressão suficiente. Há mais de 30 anos, físicos previram que, esmagada com força extrema, a água viraria um material superiônico, meio sólido e meio líquido. Os átomos de oxigênio formam uma rede cristalina, enquanto os núcleos de hidrogênio, os prótons, circulam livres por ela como um líquido. Isso torna esse gelo quase tão bom condutor de eletricidade quanto um metal, e ele seria preto. Em 2019, uma equipe do laboratório Lawrence Livermore usou seis feixes de laser gigantes para mandar ondas de choque por uma camada fina de água, a pressões de 1 a 4 milhões de vezes a do nível do mar e temperatura de metade da superfície do Sol. Flashes de raios X, disparados no momento exato, mostraram que o oxigênio tinha se arrumado em cristal, e a equipe propôs chamar a nova forma de gelo XVIII. Um físico de fora pediu mais testes para comprovar de vez o caráter superiônico. Se essa camada existe nos gigantes de gelo, ela pode ajudar a explicar os campos magnéticos tortos de Urano e Netuno.

fontes.titulo: Bizarre form of hot ice seen on Earth (National Geographic, 2019)
fontes.trecho: As the team reports today in the journal Nature, this ice exists at pressures between one and four million times that at sea level and temperatures half as hot as the surface of the sun. “Yes, we’re talking about ice,” says study leader Marius Millot, a physicist at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California. “But the sample is at several thousand degrees.” [...] And more than 30 years ago, physicists predicted that crushing pressure should squeeze water into superionic forms. Superionic materials are dual beasts, part solid and part liquid [...] In water—aka H2O—the oxygen atoms would crunch into a solidified crystal while the hydrogen’s protons would zip around like a liquid. [...] In their latest tests, the researchers used six giant laser beams to generate a sequence of shockwaves that crunched a thin layer of liquid water into solidified ice at millions of times Earth’s surface pressure and between 3,000 and 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Precisely timed x-ray flashes probed the configuration, which again only lasted for a few billionths of a second, and revealed that the oxygen atoms had indeed taken on a crystalline form. [...] The team has proposed calling this new formation Ice XVIII. While there was some overlap in conditions between the team’s two experiments, more investigations will be necessary to definitively prove that the ice is superionic, says Roberto Car, a Princeton University physicist who was not involved in the work. [...] The new experiments indicate that Uranus and Neptune should have a superionic ice layer that acts like our planet’s mantle [...] And that could help explain why they have unusual magnetic fields.

In superionic water, water molecules break apart and the oxygen ions crystallize into an evenly spaced lattice while the hydrogen ions float around freely within the oxygen lattice. The freely mobile hydrogen ions make superionic water almost as conductive as typical metals, making it a superionic conductor. The ice appears black in color. [...] The first definitive evidence for the crystal structure of the oxygen lattice in superionic water came from x-ray measurements on laser-shocked water which were reported in 2019.

gancho: A matéria mais quente já criada, uma sopa de quarks feita no CERN em 2012 a mais de 5 trilhões de graus, não se comporta como gás: esse tipo de matéria flui como um líquido quase perfeito, quase sem atrito interno.
explicacao: Prótons e nêutrons são feitos de partículas menores, os quarks, colados por glúons. Acima de cerca de 1,66 trilhão de kelvin, esses blocos "derretem" e os quarks e glúons ficam soltos num plasma. Acredita-se que o universo inteiro esteve nesse estado logo depois do Big Bang. Para recriá-lo, o experimento ALICE, no Grande Colisor de Hádrons, choca íons de chumbo a 99% da velocidade da luz. Em 13 de agosto de 2012, a equipe anunciou ter passado de 5 trilhões de kelvin, talvez 5,5 trilhões, uns 38% acima do recorde anterior, de 4 trilhões, obtido em 2010 nos EUA. O porta-voz avisou que a medida ainda era bastante incerta. A surpresa maior tinha vindo antes: os teóricos esperavam algo parecido com um gás de partículas livres, mas experimentos no colisor RHIC, nos EUA, mostraram em 2005 que o plasma se comporta como líquido. Os experimentos do RHIC indicaram que ele resiste menos ao escoamento do que qualquer outra substância conhecida: é o líquido mais perfeito já observado em laboratório.

fontes.trecho: On 13 August 2012 scientists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider, Geneva, Switzerland, announced that they had achieved temperatures of over 5 trillion K and perhaps as high as 5.5 trillion K. The team had been using the ALICE experiment to smash together lead ions at 99% of the speed of light to create a quark gluon plasma – an exotic state of matter believed to have filled the universe just after the Big Bang.

fontes.titulo: Hot stuff: CERN physicists create record-breaking subatomic soup (Nature blogs, 2012)
fontes.trecho: have achieved the hottest manmade temperatures ever, by colliding lead ions to momentarily create a quark–gluon plasma [...] say that they have achieved a quark–gluon plasma 38% hotter than a record 4-trillion-degree plasma achieved in 2010 by a similar experiment at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, which had been anointed the Guinness record holder. ALICE spokesman Paolo Giubellino says that the team’s measurement is relatively uncertain

It is a very low viscosity liquid composed of the elementary particles, quarks and gluons [...] A series of Au-Au collision studies from the RHIC published in 2005 showed that the collisions produce something like a liquid in contrast to early theoretical models. [...] RHIC experiments have shown that this is the most perfect liquid ever observed in any laboratory experiment at any scale. The new phase of matter, consisting of dissolved hadrons, exhibits less resistance to flow than any other known substance. [...] the resulting matter does not behave as a quasi-ideal state of free quarks and gluons, but, rather, as an almost perfect dense fluid. [...] which amounts to a temperature exceeding 1.66 trillion K.

gancho: Clausius criou a palavra "entropia" em 1865 imitando de propósito "energia". Décadas depois, numa história não confirmada, von Neumann sugeriu o nome a Shannon porque "ninguém sabe o que a entropia é de verdade".
explicacao: O físico alemão Rudolf Clausius, um dos fundadores da termodinâmica, precisava de um nome para a grandeza que mede, grosso modo, a energia que se perde para o trabalho útil. Preferiu buscar nas línguas antigas, para que o termo significasse o mesmo em todos os idiomas vivos, e partiu da palavra grega para "transformação", tropé. Depois explicou que escolheu "entropia" para soar parecida com "energia", porque as duas grandezas seriam muito análogas no sentido físico. O físico Leon Cooper comentou, com ironia, que assim Clausius cunhou uma palavra que significava a mesma coisa para todo mundo: nada. A palavra ganhou outro destino no século XX. Claude Shannon, ao criar a teoria da informação, procurava nome para a sua medida de incerteza e pensou em "informação" ou "incerteza". Segundo um dos relatos que circulam, von Neumann o aconselhou a usar "entropia" por dois motivos: a fórmula já existia com esse nome na mecânica estatística, e, mais importante, como ninguém sabe o que a entropia é de verdade, num debate ele sempre levaria vantagem. A história, porém, não é confirmada: ela muda conforme quem a conta, existe outra versão com palavras diferentes, e a fonte observa que, no começo, Shannon parecia não ter muita noção da semelhança com a termodinâmica.

fontes.trecho: In 1865, German physicist Rudolf Clausius, one of the leading founders of the field of thermodynamics [...] I prefer going to the ancient languages for the names of important scientific quantities, so that they may mean the same thing in all living tongues. I propose, therefore, to call S the entropy of a body, after the Greek word "transformation". I have designedly coined the word entropy to be similar to energy, for these two quantities are so analogous in their physical significance, that an analogy of denominations seems to me helpful. Leon Cooper added that in this way "he succeeded in coining a word that meant the same thing to everybody: nothing". [...] From the prefix en-, as in 'energy', and from the Greek word τροπή [tropē], which is translated in an established lexicon as turning or change

that Shannon was not particularly aware of the close similarity between his new quantity and earlier work in thermodynamics. [...] During their discussions, regarding what Shannon should call the "measure of uncertainty" or attenuation in phone-line signals with reference to his new information theory, according to one source: My greatest concern was what to call it. I thought of calling it ‘information’, but the word was overly used, so I decided to call it ‘uncertainty’. When I discussed it with John von Neumann, he had a better idea. Von Neumann told me, ‘You should call it entropy, for two reasons: In the first place your uncertainty function has been used in statistical mechanics under that name, so it already has a name. In the second place, and more important, nobody knows what entropy really is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage. According to another source, when von Neumann asked him how he was getting on with his information theory

gancho: Lord Kelvin calculou a idade da Terra pelo tempo que ela levaria para esfriar e chegou a 20 a 40 milhões de anos. Faltaram a radioatividade, então desconhecida, e o calor levado pela convecção no manto.
explicacao: Em 1862, William Thomson, o futuro Lord Kelvin, supôs que a Terra nasceu toda derretida e calculou quanto tempo ela levaria para chegar ao ritmo atual de aumento da temperatura com a profundidade. A primeira estimativa ia de 20 a 400 milhões de anos. Com o tempo, ele a estreitou: em 1897, disse que a Terra tinha mais de 20 e menos de 40 milhões de anos, provavelmente mais perto de 20. O cálculo deixava de fora duas coisas. Uma era o calor gerado pela radioatividade, processo ainda desconhecido. A outra, mais importante, era a convecção no interior do planeta, que mantém o manto superior quente por muito mais tempo. Em 1895, John Perry já contestava as suposições de Kelvin sobre a condução do calor. Em 1904, Ernest Rutherford, que falava sobre radioatividade, viu Kelvin na plateia, notou o velho físico acordar na parte crítica e saiu-se com elegância: Kelvin teria limitado a idade da Terra "desde que nenhuma nova fonte fosse descoberta", e essa fonte era o rádio. Hoje, com datação radiométrica de meteoritos, a idade estimada é de 4,54 bilhões de anos.

fontes.trecho: The age of Earth is estimated to be 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years. [...] Estimates are based on radiometric dating of meteoritic material [...] In 1862, the physicist William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin published calculations that fixed the age of Earth at between 20 million and 400 million years. He assumed that Earth had formed as a completely molten object, and determined the amount of time it would take for the near-surface temperature gradient to decrease to its present value. His calculations did not account for heat produced via radioactive decay (a then unknown process) or, more significantly, convection inside Earth, which allows the temperature in the upper mantle to remain high much longer [...] In 1895 John Perry challenged Kelvin's figure on the basis of his assumptions on conductivity [...] The last estimate Kelvin gave, in 1897, was: "that it was more than 20 and less than 40 million year old, and probably much nearer 20 than 40". [...] Rutherford wrote of addressing a meeting of the Royal Institution in 1904: I came into the room, which was half dark, and presently spotted Lord Kelvin in the audience and realized that I was in trouble at the last part of my speech dealing with the age of the Earth, where my views conflicted with his. To my relief, Kelvin fell fast asleep, but as I came to the important point, I saw the old bird sit up, open an eye, and cock a baleful glance at me! Then a sudden inspiration came, and I said, "Lord Kelvin had limited the age of the Earth, provided no new source was discovered. That prophetic utterance refers to what we are now considering tonight, radium!"

gancho: Por séculos se disse que o alho estragava a bússola. No século XVI, um italiano testou com o próprio bafo e os marinheiros riram da ideia. Mesmo assim, há relatos de timoneiros britânicos açoitados por comer alho.
explicacao: A crendice é antiga: Plutarco e, depois dele, o astrônomo Ptolomeu escreveram de passagem que o alho anulava a força de atração do ímã. Daí nasceu o boato de que os marinheiros eram proibidos de comer alho e cebola, para que o cheiro não deixasse a bússola inútil. O italiano Giambattista della Porta resolveu conferir: soprou hálito de alho sobre uma pedra-ímã e nada mudou. Ao perguntar aos próprios marinheiros, ouviu que aquilo era conversa de velhas e que gente do mar preferia perder a vida a ficar sem cebola e alho. Em 1600, o inglês William Gilbert, no livro De Magnete, tratou como "fábula e falsidade" a ideia de que um ímã esfregado com alho perde o poder. A obra se apoiava em experimento e observação, e não em ouvir dizer. Nem isso bastou. Segundo uma resenha publicada num site da NASA, só mais de cem anos depois do livro de Gilbert deixou de ser falta punida com chibatadas, para um timoneiro da marinha britânica, ter bafo de alho, pelo medo de desmagnetizar a bússola do navio.

fontes.trecho: One belief, dating back to Pliny, was that fumes from heating garlic and onions could destroy the magnetism in a compass, rendering it useless. Even after William Gilbert disproved this in 1600, there were reports of helmsmen on British ships being flogged for eating garlic. However, this belief was far from universal. In 1558 Giambattista della Porta reported

fontes.titulo: Laws of Attraction (Science History Institute, Distillations)
fontes.trecho: Plutarch, and the astronomer Ptolemy after him, drew attention to the magnet’s attractive power, noting in passing that garlic had the ability to neutralize it. This belief would later spawn the rumor that mariners were forbidden to eat garlic or onions lest their compass be rendered inoperable. [...] della Porta showed experimentally that garlic had no effect on a lodestone (he breathed garlic breath on it). He also consulted with sailors who answered that “they were old Wives fables, and things ridiculous; and that Sea-men would sooner lose their lives, then abstain from eating Onyons and Garlick.”

fontes.titulo: Review of De Magnete (NASA Goddard, The Great Magnet, the Earth)
fontes.trecho: based on experiment and observation rather than hearsay, being practised twenty years before the publication of Bacon's Novum Organum. And, over a hundred years before it ceased to be an offence punishable by flogging for a British naval helmsman to have garlic on his breath for fear of demagnetising the ship's compass, De Magnete dismisses as "fable and falsehood" the idea that a lodestone smeared with garlic loses its power.

gancho: Em 1746, um abade francês ligou centenas de monges com pedaços de fio de ferro, numa grande roda, e descarregou neles um choque. Todos reagiram quase juntos: a eletricidade se propagava muito rápido.
explicacao: O choque vinha de uma novidade da época, a garrafa de Leyden, descoberta de forma independente pelo alemão Ewald von Kleist em 1745 e pelo holandês Pieter van Musschenbroek, de Leiden, entre 1745 e 1746. Ela foi o primeiro meio de acumular muita carga elétrica e soltá-la quando o experimentador quisesse. Musschenbroek contou o experimento numa carta, e o abade Jean-Antoine Nollet confirmou o resultado e leu a carta numa sessão pública da Academia de Paris, em abril de 1746. No mesmo ano, para o rei Luís XV, Nollet descarregou uma garrafa através de 180 guardas reais e, depois, de um número maior de monges cartuxos, que pularam praticamente ao mesmo tempo. Na versão mais conhecida (os números variam entre os relatos), eram uns duzentos monges numa roda de cerca de 1,6 km de circunferência, unidos por fios de ferro, e o choque vinha de uma bateria de garrafas. Como cada homem reagiu quase no mesmo instante, ficou claro que a eletricidade corria pelo circuito com enorme velocidade. Do que acharam o rei e os voluntários, não ficou registro.

fontes.trecho: In 1746 Nollet gathered about two hundred monks into a circle about a mile (1.6 km) in circumference, with pieces of iron wire connecting them. He then discharged a battery of Leyden jars through the human chain and observed that each man reacted at substantially the same time to the electric shock, showing that the speed of electricity's propagation was very high.

Its invention was a discovery made independently by German cleric Ewald Georg von Kleist on 11 October 1745 and by Dutch scientist Pieter van Musschenbroek of Leiden (Leyden), Netherlands, in 1745–1746. [...] It was the first means of accumulating and preserving electric charge in large quantities that could be discharged at the experimenter's will [...] Abbé Jean-Antoine Nollet read this report, confirmed the experiment, and then read Musschenbroek's letter in a public meeting of the Paris Academy in April 1746 [...] In 1746, Abbé Nollet performed two experiments for the edification of King Louis XV of France, in the first of which he discharged a Leyden jar through 180 royal guardsmen, and in the second through a larger number of Carthusian monks, all of whom sprang into the air more or less simultaneously. The opinions of neither the king nor the experimental subjects have been recorded.

gancho: A pipa de Franklin não foi atingida por um raio, ao contrário do que se conta: se fosse, ele provavelmente se feriria gravemente ou morreria. Em 1753, um físico em São Petersburgo morreu numa experiência parecida.
explicacao: Em 1752, Benjamin Franklin propôs usar hastes condutoras para levar a eletricidade dos raios a uma garrafa de Leyden, mas a Filadélfia não tinha torre alta o bastante. Quem fez o teste primeiro foi o francês Thomas-François Dalibard, em maio de 1752, em Marly-la-Ville. Franklin teve a ideia de erguer a haste com uma pipa. Pelo relato de Joseph Priestley, de 1767, o voo foi em junho de 1752, com a ajuda do filho William. Nenhum raio caiu na pipa: a nuvem carregada induziu carga na pipa e na linha de cânhamo molhada, os fiapos soltos passaram a se repelir e, ao aproximar a mão da chave presa à linha, Franklin tirou uma faísca. Em agosto de 1753, o físico Georg Wilhelm Richmann tentava medir a resposta de uma haste isolada a uma tempestade próxima quando uma descarga, descrita como um raio globular, o atingiu na cabeça. Ficou com uma mancha vermelha na testa, o sapato esquerdo estourado e roupas chamuscadas. A explosão deixou desacordado o gravurista que o acompanhava e arrancou a porta das dobradiças. Richmann parece ter sido a primeira pessoa a morrer fazendo experimentos com eletricidade.

fontes.trecho: In 1752, Franklin proposed an experiment with conductive rods to attract lightning to a Leyden jar, an early form of capacitor, but there was no spire in Philadelphia that was high enough for him to attempt it. Thomas-François Dalibard, however, did carry out such an experiment in Northern France in May 1752 at Marly-la-Ville. Then the following years, an attempt to replicate the experiment killed Georg Wilhelm Richmann in Saint Petersburg in August 1753 [...] Franklin conceived the idea of using a kite to raise the lightning rod to a great height. [...] The fullest account of Franklin's actual experiment was given by Joseph Priestley in his 1767 treatise [...] According to Priestley, Franklin's experiment took place in June 1752, when he flew a kite during a thunderstorm with the assistance of his son William Franklin. [...] Contrary to popular belief, Franklin's kite was not struck by lightning, which would probably have resulted in serious injury or death. Instead, an electrical charge was induced on the kite by its proximity to an oppositely charged storm cloud. Franklin noticed that loose threads of the string were repelling one another [...] He also approached his hand to the key, which resulted in an electrical spark.

Richmann was electrocuted in Saint Petersburg on 6 August 1753 (Old Style, 26 July 1753) while "trying to quantify the response of an insulated rod to a nearby storm." [...] a discharge reported to have been ball lightning appeared and collided with Richmann's head leaving him with a red spot on his forehead, his left shoe blown open, and parts of his clothes singed. [...] An explosion followed "like that of a small Cannon" that knocked the engraver out, split the room's door frame, and tore the door off its hinges. [...] Richmann appears to be the first person in history to have lost his life while conducting electrical experiments.

gancho: Em 1803, em Londres, o sobrinho de Galvani aplicou eletricidade no corpo de um condenado executado. A mandíbula tremeu, um olho se abriu e a mão se fechou, e muitos acharam que o morto ia voltar à vida.
explicacao: Giovanni Aldini, nascido em Bolonha em 1762, era sobrinho de Luigi Galvani, pioneiro dos estudos com eletricidade, e trabalhou no laboratório do tio com experimentos de contração muscular. Como o tio, acreditava num "suco elétrico" produzido no cérebro e levado pelos nervos até os músculos. Para mostrar que a corrente podia reanimar músculos de animais e pessoas mortas, fez demonstrações públicas. A mais famosa foi em Newgate, em 1803, com o corpo do criminoso George Forster. Segundo o relato do Newgate Calendar, ao primeiro estímulo no rosto, as mandíbulas começaram a tremer, os músculos em volta se contorceram de forma horrível e um olho chegou a se abrir. Depois, a mão direita se ergueu e se fechou, e as pernas se mexeram. Muitos espectadores acharam que o morto estava prestes a reviver. Mary Shelley tinha só 5 anos na época, e já se sugeriu que Aldini possa ter inspirado o seu Victor Frankenstein. Ela não o cita na introdução da edição de 1831, mas conta que o "galvanismo" estava entre os assuntos das conversas antes do "sonho acordado" que deu origem ao livro.

fontes.trecho: Giovanni Aldini was born in Bologna on 10 April 1762. He was the nephew of the renowned scientist Luigi Galvani, a pioneer in electrical research [...] he began working as a research assistant in Galvani's laboratory in Bologna, focusing on muscle contraction experiments. [...] Like his uncle, Aldini was a vitalist who believed in the existence of an electrical juice generated in the brain and flowing through the nerves to supply the muscles with power. [...] to prove that electric current could reanimate muscle tissue in deceased animals and humans. Aldini's most famous public demonstration of the electro-stimulation technique of deceased limbs was performed on the executed criminal George Forster at Newgate in London in 1803. The electrical stimulation created such violent movements in the corpse that many onlookers believed the dead man was on the verge of returning to life. [...] On the first application of the process to the face, the jaws of the deceased criminal began to quiver, and the adjoining muscles were horribly contorted, and one eye was actually opened. In the subsequent part of the process, the right hand was raised and clenched, and the legs and thighs were set in motion. [...] Although Mary Shelley was just 5 years old when Forster was executed, it has been suggested that Aldini might have been the inspiration for her famous fictional character Victor Frankenstein. [...] In her introduction to the 1831 edition of Frankenstein, she does not mention Aldini, but "galvanism" was among the evening discussion topics before she experienced her "waking dream" that led to her writing.

gancho: Michael Faraday, que descobriu a indução eletromagnética e criou o ancestral dos geradores, não ia além da álgebra mais simples. Aprendiz de encadernador, entrou na ciência mandando anotações a um químico famoso.
explicacao: Faraday teve só a educação escolar mais básica e precisou estudar sozinho. Aos 14 anos virou aprendiz de um encadernador e livreiro de Londres, e nos sete anos de aprendizado leu muitos dos livros que passavam pela oficina. Em 1812, aos 20 anos, assistiu a palestras de Humphry Davy, da Royal Institution, e depois lhe mandou um livro de 300 páginas feito com as notas que tomara. A resposta de Davy foi imediata e gentil e, em 1813, depois de ferir a vista num acidente com tricloreto de nitrogênio, ele contratou Faraday como assistente. Em 1831, Faraday começou a série de experimentos em que descobriu a indução eletromagnética, e com esses princípios construiu o dínamo elétrico. Ele pensava o mundo de forma visual, em linhas de força, e não em símbolos: sua matemática não chegava à trigonometria. Foi James Clerk Maxwell quem resumiu esse trabalho, e o de outros, nas equações que são a base das teorias modernas do eletromagnetismo. Sobre as linhas de força, Maxwell escreveu que elas mostravam Faraday como, na realidade, um matemático de altíssimo nível. Einstein mantinha um retrato dele na parede do escritório, ao lado dos de Newton e Maxwell.

fontes.trecho: The young Michael Faraday, having only the most basic school education, had to educate himself. At the age of 14 he became an apprentice to George Riebau, a local bookbinder and bookseller in Blandford Street. During his seven-year apprenticeship Faraday read many books [...] In 1812, at the age of 20 and at the end of his apprenticeship, Faraday attended lectures by the eminent English chemist Humphry Davy of the Royal Institution [...] Faraday subsequently sent Davy a 300-page book based on notes that he had taken during these lectures. Davy's reply was immediate, kind, and favourable. In 1813, when Davy damaged his eyesight in an accident with nitrogen trichloride, he decided to hire Michael Faraday as an assistant. [...] in 1831, he began his great series of experiments in which he discovered electromagnetic induction [...] Faraday would later use the principles he had discovered to construct the electric dynamo, the ancestor of modern power generators and the electric motor. [...] thought and sensed the physical world in a visual manner, rather than in words or symbols. His mathematical abilities did not extend as far as trigonometry and were limited to the simplest algebra. Physicist and mathematician James Clerk Maxwell took the work of Faraday and others and summarised it in a set of equations which is accepted as the basis of all modern theories of electromagnetic phenomena. On Faraday's uses of lines of force, Maxwell wrote that they show Faraday "to have been in reality a mathematician of a very high order [...] Albert Einstein kept a portrait of Faraday on his study wall, alongside those of Isaac Newton and Maxwell.

gancho: As quatro "equações de Maxwell" dos livros não foram escritas assim por Maxwell, que usou 20 equações com 20 variáveis. A forma enxuta é de Oliver Heaviside, um telegrafista que só pôde estudar na escola até os 16 anos.
explicacao: Depois dos 16 anos, Heaviside não teve mais nenhum ensino formal: era um aluno de destaque, mas a família não conseguiu mantê-lo na escola, e ele passou mais um ano estudando por conta própria. O trabalho veio por um parente. O tio por casamento Charles Wheatstone, um dos inventores do primeiro telégrafo que deu certo no comércio, mandou o sobrinho em 1867 para Newcastle, numa das suas empresas de telégrafo, e dois anos depois o rapaz já era operador de telégrafo. Em 1873, caiu-lhe nas mãos o tratado de Maxwell em dois volumes, recém-lançado. Pelas palavras dele, sabia só a álgebra e a trigonometria da escola, quase esquecidas, e precisou de anos para entender a obra. No mesmo ano, a Sociedade de Engenheiros de Telégrafo barrou sua entrada, alegando não querer "funcionários de telégrafo". Em 1884, ele deu à teoria a roupa que ela veste até hoje: com o rotacional e o divergente do cálculo vetorial, condensou 12 das 20 equações de Maxwell em apenas quatro. E as duas versões não são idênticas: a de Heaviside é até mais fácil de adaptar à física quântica. Na velhice, conforme o relato de um colega, fugia tanto de gente que deixava os manuscritos numa mercearia para os editores buscarem. Punha "W.O.R.M." depois do nome nas cartas e, conta-se, pintava as unhas de rosa e mobiliou a casa com blocos de granito. Em 1922, a recém-criada Medalha Faraday teve nele o seu primeiro premiado.

fontes.trecho: He was a good student, placing fifth out of five hundred pupils in 1865, but his parents could not keep him at school after he was 16, so he continued studying for a year by himself and had no further formal education. Heaviside's uncle by marriage was Sir Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875), an internationally celebrated expert in telegraphy and electromagnetism, and the original co-inventor of the first commercially successful telegraph in the mid-1830s. [...] Wheatstone took a strong interest in his nephew's education, and in 1867 sent him north to work with his older brother Arthur Wheatstone, who was managing one of Charles' telegraph companies in Newcastle upon Tyne. Two years later he took a job as a telegraph operator [...] Later in 1873 his application to join the Society of Telegraph Engineers was turned down with the comment that "they didn't want telegraph clerks". [...] In 1873, Heaviside had encountered Maxwell's newly published, and later famous, two-volume Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism. [...] I had no knowledge of mathematical analysis (having learned only school algebra and trigonometry which I had largely forgotten) and thus my work was laid out for me. It took me several years before I could understand as much as I possibly could. [...] In 1884 he recast Maxwell's mathematical analysis from its original cumbersome form [...] Maxwell's formulation of electromagnetism consisted of 20 equations in 20 variables. Heaviside employed the curl and divergence operators of the vector calculus to reformulate 12 of these 20 equations into four equations in four variables [...] the form by which they have been known ever since (see Maxwell's equations). Less well known is that Heaviside's equations and Maxwell's are not exactly the same, and in fact it is easier to modify the former to make them compatible with quantum physics. [...] According to associate B.A. Behrend, he became a recluse who was so averse to meeting people that he delivered the manuscripts of his Electrician papers to a grocery store, where the editors picked them up. [...] Heaviside would sign letters with the initials "W.O.R.M." after his name. Heaviside also reportedly started painting his fingernails pink and had granite rocks moved into his house for furniture. In 1922, he became the first recipient of the Faraday Medal [...] In 1922, he became the first recipient of the Faraday Medal, which was established that year.

gancho: Num fio de cobre de 2 mm com 1 ampère, os elétrons avançam uns 23 milésimos de milímetro por segundo, e no sentido oposto ao da "corrente" dos livros. Na corrente alternada, eles só vão e voltam.
explicacao: Quando se liga um aparelho, o que corre depressa não são os elétrons, e sim o sinal: ele viaja como onda eletromagnética em volta dos condutores, em geral entre 50% e 99% da velocidade da luz no vácuo. Os elétrons livres do metal até se agitam muito rápido, mas em direções aleatórias. O campo elétrico só acrescenta a isso um pequeno avanço médio, a velocidade de deriva. Numa conta feita na Wikipedia, para um fio de cobre de 2 mm de diâmetro levando 1 ampère, ela dá cerca de 23 micrômetros por segundo. Com corrente alternada de 60 Hz, não há deslocamento líquido: em meio ciclo, os elétrons derivam em média menos de 0,2 micrômetro e depois voltam. E ainda andam "ao contrário". Antes de se conhecerem prótons e elétrons, Benjamin Franklin definiu como positiva a carga que um bastão de vidro ganha ao ser esfregado em seda. A escolha do sinal era arbitrária, e o sentido convencional da corrente ficou sendo o do movimento das cargas positivas. Nos fios de metal, porém, quem se move são os elétrons, de carga negativa, que andam no sentido oposto ao da seta desenhada nos circuitos.

fontes.trecho: Assume a current I = 1 ampere, and a wire of 2 mm diameter (radius = 0.001 m). [...] Therefore, in this wire, the electrons are flowing at the rate of 23 μm/s. At 60 Hz alternating current, this means that, within half a cycle (1/120th sec.), on average the electrons drift less than 0.2 μm. [...] there is a definite small drift velocity of electrons, which is superimposed on the random motion of free electrons. [...] The drift speed of electrons is generally in the order of 10−3 meters per second whereas the thermal speed is on the order of 106 meters per second.

In everyday electrical and electronic devices, signals (such as a pulse) travel as electromagnetic waves around the conductors typically at 50%–99% of the speed of light in vacuum. However, the electrons themselves move much more slowly [...] Alternating current causes no net movement. The electrons travel back and forth with the alternating electric potential.

Before these particles were discovered, a positive charge was defined by Benjamin Franklin as the charge acquired by a glass rod when it is rubbed with a silk cloth. [...] it is arbitrary which type of charge is called positive and which is called negative.

The conventional direction of current, also known as conventional current, is arbitrarily defined as the direction in which positive charges flow. [...] So, in metals where the charge carriers (electrons) are negative, conventional current is in the opposite direction to the overall electron movement.

gancho: Numa bobina de um gravímetro na Bélgica, uma corrente elétrica circulou sem bateria nem gerador de 1995 a pelo menos 2017, 22 anos seguidos. Experimentos indicam que correntes assim durariam ao menos 100 mil anos.
explicacao: Lord Kelvin argumentava que, em temperaturas baixas o bastante, a resistência elétrica de qualquer material cresceria sem limite. Foi isso que levou o holandês Heike Kamerlingh Onnes a estudar a resistência perto do zero absoluto, usando o hélio líquido que acabara de ser produzido. Em 8 de abril de 1911, ao esfriar mercúrio sólido a 4,2 kelvin, ele viu a resistência sumir de repente: tinha descoberto a supercondutividade, e Kelvin estava errado. Abaixo da temperatura crítica, uma corrente posta para girar num anel supercondutor pode continuar indefinidamente, sem bateria nem gerador, e é isso que se aproveita nos eletroímãs das máquinas de ressonância magnética. Para correntes assim em geral, experimentos indicam uma duração de pelo menos 100 mil anos, e estimativas teóricas podem passar do tempo de vida estimado do universo. Um caso real fica em Membach, na Bélgica. Num gravímetro supercondutor, bobinas de fio de nióbio mantêm suspensa uma esfera de nióbio de 4 gramas, do tamanho de uma bola de pingue-pongue, a menos de 9,2 kelvin. O aparelho foi ligado em 4 de agosto de 1995 e, em 18 de setembro de 2017, completou 8.081 dias de medição contínua, um recorde mundial. A corrente injetada em 1995 nunca tinha se dissipado. Os próprios pesquisadores lembram que isso não é física nova: em teoria, uma corrente supercondutora pode fluir para sempre. O fenômeno só se explica pela mecânica quântica.

fontes.trecho: An electric current through a loop of superconducting wire can persist indefinitely with no power source. [...] Like ferromagnetism and atomic spectral lines, superconductivity is a phenomenon which can only be explained by quantum mechanics. [...] a property exploited in superconducting electromagnets such as those found in MRI machines. Experiments have demonstrated that currents in superconducting coils can persist for years without any measurable degradation. Experimental evidence points to a lifetime of at least 100,000 years. Theoretical estimates for the lifetime of a persistent current can exceed the estimated lifetime of the universe, depending on the wire geometry and the temperature. [...] Lord Kelvin had argued, using the law of corresponding states, that the resistivity of all substances diverges at sufficiently low temperatures. This argument influenced Onnes to investigate the low temperature limit of resistivity. Onnes result would later go onto prove Kelvin incorrect. Superconductivity was discovered in solid mercury on April 8, 1911, by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, who was studying the resistance of mercury at cryogenic temperatures using the recently produced liquid helium as a refrigerant. At the temperature of 4.2 K, he observed that the resistance abruptly disappeared.

The niobium sphere, about the size of a ping-pong ball, is encased in a metal cylinder [...] As long as the temperature inside the container is kept below 9.2 K, niobium’s superconducting transition temperature [...] Niobium wire coils, also kept at this low temperature, offer no resistance to the electrical current that flows through them, producing the perfectly stable magnetic field that levitates the niobium sphere. [...] On 18 September 2017, this instrument, which began operation 4 August 1995, had monitored gravity changes continuously for 8,081 days—22 years and 45 days. [...] In 1995, currents were injected into the superconducting coils, causing the sphere to levitate. More than 22 years later, the currents persist. The SG measurement principle is based on monitoring the levitation of a 4-gram superconducting niobium sphere. [...] This isn’t new physics—in theory, a superconducting current can flow forever

fontes.titulo: World record in the underground laboratory of Membach (Royal Observatory of Belgium, 2017)
fontes.trecho: World record in the underground laboratory of Membach: A sphere of mass 4 grams has been levitating for 8081 days [...] The total duration is 22 years and 45 days, or 8081 days. [...] In 1995, currents were injected into superconducting coils causing the sphere to levitate; the currents have never been dissipated ever since.

gancho: Um físico fez uma rã viva flutuar no ar só com um ímã muito forte e ganhou o Ig Nobel, prêmio para pesquisas que fazem rir. Dez anos depois, levou o Nobel de Física pelo grafeno. Foi o primeiro a ter os dois.
explicacao: O truque usa o diamagnetismo, uma resposta magnética que faz o material ser repelido por um campo. Água, madeira e a maioria dos compostos orgânicos são diamagnéticos, e o efeito é tão fraco que não se nota no dia a dia. Com um ímã potente, porém, um corpo cheio de água pode flutuar em equilíbrio estável. O teorema de Earnshaw, que parece proibir esse tipo de levitação estática, só vale para materiais atraídos pelo campo, como os ferromagnéticos. Em 1997, ao investigar efeitos do magnetismo na água, Andre Geim conseguiu levitar água e depois uma pequena rã, num trabalho publicado com Michael Berry no European Journal of Physics. Os dois ganharam o Ig Nobel de Física em 2000, e Geim se orgulhou de terem tido humor para aceitar. Em 2010, ele dividiu com Konstantin Novoselov o Nobel de Física por experimentos com o grafeno, um material bidimensional. Entrou no Guinness como a primeira pessoa a ganhar, individualmente, os dois prêmios, e diz que dá a ambos o mesmo valor. Em 2001, ainda pôs como coautor de um artigo seu hamster favorito, H.A.M.S. ter Tisha.

fontes.trecho: He is the first and only individual, as of 2026, to have received both Nobel and Ig Nobel prizes, for which he holds a Guinness World Record. [...] Geim's research in 1997 into the possible effects of magnetism on water scaling led to the famous discovery of direct diamagnetic levitation of water, and led to a frog being levitated. For this experiment, he and Michael Berry received the 2000 Ig Nobel Prize. "We were asked first whether we dared to accept this prize, and I take pride in our sense of humor and self-deprecation that we did". [...] levitate a small frog with magnets, which he and Berry reported in the European Journal of Physics in 1997. [...] On 5 October 2010, Geim was awarded the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics jointly with Novoselov "for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene". [...] "Frankly, I value both my Ig Nobel prize and Nobel prize at the same level [...] 2010, Geim was inducted into the Guinness World Records as the "First individual to win both a Nobel and Ig Nobel prize". [...] He named his favourite hamster, H.A.M.S. ter Tisha, co-author in a 2001 research paper.

Diamagnetism is a form of magnetic response in materials that describes the property being repelled by an applied magnetic field [...] Diamagnetic materials are those that some people generally think of as non-magnetic, and include water, wood, most organic compounds [...] However, since diamagnetism is such a weak property, its effects are not observable in everyday life. [...] Diamagnets may be levitated in stable equilibrium in a magnetic field, with no power consumption. Earnshaw's theorem seems to preclude the possibility of static magnetic levitation. However, Earnshaw's theorem applies only to objects with positive susceptibilities, such as ferromagnets [...] Most spectacularly, a live frog (see figure) was levitated.

gancho: A elefanta Topsy, morta com eletricidade em 1903, não foi vítima de Thomas Edison na "guerra das correntes". Ele não estava lá, e essa disputa tinha acabado dez anos antes. A confusão veio de um filme e de um nome.
explicacao: Topsy era uma elefanta asiática de circo que acabou no Luna Park, em Coney Island, Nova York. Os donos do parque, Thompson e Dundy, anunciaram que a enforcariam em público e cobrariam ingresso, mas a sociedade protetora dos animais, a ASPCA, proibiu. Em 4 de janeiro de 1903, diante de convidados e repórteres, ela comeu cenouras com 460 gramas de cianeto de potássio, levou um choque elétrico e foi estrangulada por cordas grossas puxadas por um guincho a vapor. O choque foi a causa final da morte. A parte elétrica ficou com a companhia de energia local, que tinha "Edison" no nome, mas já não tinha relação com a antiga empresa dele. Uma equipe da produtora de filmes de Edison gravou 74 segundos da cena, lançados como "Electrocuting an Elephant", provavelmente a primeira morte de um animal filmada. Edison nunca esteve no parque e, na época, já estava fora do negócio de iluminação elétrica. A lenda nasceu de jornais que falavam em "eletricistas da Edison Company" e do crédito "Thomas A. Edison" que aparecia na tela dos filmes da produtora, feitos com pouca ou nenhuma participação dele.

fontes.trecho: Topsy (c. 1875 – January 4, 1903) was a female Asian elephant who was electrocuted to death at Coney Island, New York, in January 1903. [...] On January 4, 1903, in front of a small crowd of invited reporters and guests, Topsy was fed carrots laced with 460 grams of potassium cyanide, electrocuted and strangled, the electrocution being the final cause of death. Among the invited press that day was a crew from Edison Studios who filmed the event. Their film of the electrocution part was released to be viewed in coin-operated kinetoscopes under the title Electrocuting an Elephant. It is probably the first filmed death of an animal in history. [...] with false claims that it was an anti–alternating current demonstration organized by Thomas Edison during the war of the currents. Edison was never at Luna Park and the electrocution of Topsy took place ten years after the end of the war of currents. [...] On January 1, 1903, Thompson and Dundy announced plans to conduct a public hanging of the elephant, set for January 3 or 4, and collect a 25¢ a head admission [...] strangling the elephant with large ropes tied to a steam-powered winch [...] The crew shot a 74-second film of Topsy's electrocution. [...] At the time of Topsy's death, Edison was no longer involved in the electric lighting business [...] privately owned Brooklyn power company named "Edison" mentioned in contemporaneous newspaper reports was no longer associated with the earlier Edison Illuminating Company. Edison himself was not present at Luna Park when the film was made and the more than 1,200 short films from the Edison Manufacturing film company from this period were made with very little to no input from Edison. [...] describing it as being carried out by "electricians of the Edison Company” (leading to the eventual confusing of the unrelated power company with the man), and the fact that the film of the event (like most Edison films from that period) was credited onscreen to "Thomas A. Edison"

gancho: Humboldt relatou ter visto, em 1800, poraquês saltando da água para dar choques em cavalos. Em 200 anos não houve registro científico parecido, e cogitou-se exagero. Um estudo de 2016 mostrou o salto em laboratório.
explicacao: O naturalista Alexander von Humboldt acompanhou indígenas que pescavam poraquês usando cavalos: uns trinta animais foram tocados para dentro da água. O pisoteio fazia os peixes, de até 1,5 m, saírem da lama e atacar, erguendo-se para fora da água para dar descargas. Ele viu dois cavalos ficarem atordoados e se afogarem. Depois de tantos choques, os poraquês, esgotados, nadaram para a margem e foram apanhados com arpões. Nos 200 anos seguintes, nenhum estudo científico descreveu algo igual. O biólogo Kenneth Catania, da Universidade Vanderbilt, achou o comportamento por acaso: transferia seus poraquês com uma rede de aro e cabo de metal e, de vez em quando, um deles parava de fugir e atacava, saltando e apertando o queixo contra o cabo enquanto disparava pulsos de alta voltagem. Medindo os ataques numa placa de alumínio, viu que a tensão e a corrente subiam muito conforme o peixe subia no alvo, porque a corrente atravessa o alvo e volta pela água até a cauda, fechando o circuito. Os ataques eram mais comuns quando o nível da água baixava, provavelmente porque os peixes se sentiam encurralados. Para Catania, é razoável supor que Humboldt viu algo assim em 19 de março de 1800.

fontes.trecho: In 1800, the explorer Alexander von Humboldt joined a group of indigenous people who went fishing with horses, some thirty of which they chased into the water. The pounding of the horses' hooves, he noted, drove the fish, up to 5 feet (1.5 m) long out of the mud and prompted them to attack, rising out of the water and using their electricity to shock the horses. He saw two horses stunned by the shocks and then drowned. The electric eels, having given many shocks, "now require long rest and plenty of nourishment to replace the loss of galvanic power they have suffered", "swam timidly to the bank of the pond", and were easily caught using small harpoons on ropes.

fontes.titulo: Electric eels make leaping attacks (Vanderbilt University, 2016)
fontes.trecho: Jun 6, 2016 [...] In the following 200 years, however, there have been no scientific reports of similar behavior on the part of the eels, suggesting that perhaps von Humboldt exaggerated. [...] Vanderbilt University biologist Kenneth Catania accidentally discovered that [...] Initially, he used a net with metal rim and handle to transfer the eels from one place to another. [...] As he scooped up the larger eels he found that every so often, an eel would stop trying to evade the net and attack it by leaping out of the water while pressing its chin to the handle, all the while generating a series of high-voltage pulses. [...] By hooking a voltmeter and then an ammeter to an aluminum plate, Catania was able to measure the nature and strength of the electric impulses the eels were producing as they leap up the conductor. He found that both the voltage and the amperage produced by the eels increased dramatically as the eel leaped higher on the target. [...] Then the electric current travels through the target until it can exit back into the water where it travels back to the eel’s tail, completing the circuit. [...] Catania found that his eels most often attacked when the water in the aquarium was lowered, probably because they felt cornered. [...] “it seems reasonable to suggest that [he] observed a similar eel behavior on March 19th of 1800,” Catania said.

gancho: Na noite de 14 de fevereiro de 1982, um detector registrou o que parecia ser um monopolo magnético, um ímã com um polo só. O sinal nunca se repetiu, e até hoje não se sabe se essa partícula existe.
